title: Working with strings and a harp behind her
summary: She says she can do without strings, compares with the Ellis Larkin trio and early harpists who swung.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Would you exempt that recording session from what you said before about recording with strings?
No -- well, that isn't exactly what I consider working with strings. The way I see working with strings would be a large orchestra with strings -- accompaniment --
Thousands of them.
Yeah, and you know, playing -- all right, take the other recording that
I made on the Joe Davis thing there, they had a couple of strings there, you know, and I hated that string accompaniment, it sounded like --
I wonder what it actually sounded like because I think the balance --
You didn't hear it?
Yes, I heard it of the scratchd78, that's what I taped it off.
I didn't like the strings but --
It didn't sound to me like they had a cello or --
No, no, no, just probably a couple of violins then a little something that somebody wrote out for them to improvise. Now if this would have been Joe Venuti --

Okay, but if there was some balance, if there was some kind of, you know, something from the lower register in there with those other fiddles then that might have been a different proposition, but it sounds very thin.
Yeah, it is very thin.

I could do without the strings, believe you me, I can do without a lot of background. I feel very, very restricted, you know, when it comes to large arrangements, anything that's arranged, you know -- boom, boom, boom.
What if somebody said -- well, I won't prejudge the issue. Remember when you were on that Women in Jazz concerts, they had the woman who plays the harp, Corky Hale, did you hear her when she played?
I don't think I was there when she played.
I was just wondering, what if somebody said to you, would you like to do some duets just with a harp behind you, just a couple of titles to see what it was like?

Look, during the days of some live programs, you know, from radio stations there was a show, it tried to be a duplicate of the Saturday Night Swing Club which was in the '30s but this was later and the producer thought of this idea, he had females, you know, the distaff side and they
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
had a harpist who was a studio musician and I did --
But was she a jazz musician because I think you would say of Corky Hale that she is actually --

Well, she was not considered a jazz musician, she was a studio musician that probably just played the arrangements, whatever they put in front of her. But on this particular show we did -- I did, just with her, 'If I Had a Ribbon Bow.'
But that's a tight arrangement --

A tight arrangement and not only that, they wrote in some fill-ins for her because my music as its written is just sort of a basic accompaniment and she didn't play the figures that were written for the orchestra, they wrote some special figures in and, you know, she was playing a lot of that. That wasn't bad, but all I did was stick to the melody. We were not swinging and I've heard some of the -- I worked on a bill with Daphne Ruban Hellman at the Le Bleu for a while. She appeared,

but I never worked with her, but I thought that she did a very good job swinging the harp. And there was another gal, too, I can't remember her name who played -- well, all right, Adele Girard?
That's right.

Yeah, one of the early harpists who swung the harp and they swung, you know, and I'm all for the musicians swinging. Look, I listen to a lot of music and I listen to a lot of styles and all that, but for me, you know, there's so much I can do and so much I can't --
I guess that sort of proves where you draw the limit in your art.
